Attention, Step by Step

Attention, Step by Step

How a translation model decides which source words to look at while it writes each output word. The running example is the start of our sentence: Unha tía miña, que todo o solucionaba con ditos e refráns, dicía algo así como «un é escravo do que di e dono do que cala». It continues the neural translation page, which shows how an encoder and a decoder translate without attention.

1Attention, computed by hand

Review

From the translation page, sections 2 and 3: a translation model has an encoder, which reads the Galician words, and a decoder, which writes the English words one at a time. The encoder reads the words in order and makes one vector after each word, from the vector before and the new word. Its last vector is the summary. The decoder keeps its own vector, the decoder state: it starts as the summary and takes in each English word the decoder writes.

Section 3 runs two trained translation models on our sentence, with and without attention. Their vectors have 8 numbers each, too many to follow. This section runs the same steps on a model small enough to compute by hand: the phrase unha tía miña, and vectors with three numbers, one per Galician word. We set every number by hand, to show how the calculations work in principle. In a real model, these numbers are learned in training, as in the skip-gram lesson. A vector is drawn twice: as a column of three squares with its numbers (the darker, the larger), and as a point in the picture on the right, with one axis per row.

2Query and key: try your own query

The same model as section 1. In steps 6 and 7, the encoder vectors played two parts: as keys, each was compared with the decoder's query, and the dot product gave its score; softmax turned the scores into weights; as values, the encoder vectors were added up with these weights into the mix. Set the query's three numbers, or pick one below.

Queries

The arithmetic

Attention weights

What the decoder would write with this mix

One query serves only the words that need the same Galician word: the query that finds tía gets “an aunt” right and “of mine” wrong. So the decoder makes a new query for each English word.

In this model and in the trained models of sections 3 and 4, the encoder vectors serve as both keys and values. In a transformer (sections 5 to 7), each word's vector is turned into a separate query, key and value by three sets of learned weights; the arithmetic after that is the same.

3The same steps in two trained models

Two small models translate our whole sentence. We trained them on the same data, and they are identical except for one thing: without attention, the decoder gets the summary for every English word; with attention, it gets a new mix of all the encoder's vectors for every English word, as in section 1. Their vectors have 8 dimensions, and their numbers were learned in training: every number below is the models' own. Each step links to the step of section 1 that does the same thing by hand. One difference: here the query is the decoder state itself.

−1+1one square = one dimension of a vector. Every number is between −1 and +1: each new vector of these models is a mix of the previous vector and a new candidate squashed into that range (by the tanh function), starting from zeros.

4The two models, word by word

The two models of section 3, for every word, every example sentence and three vector sizes. They were trained on the same data for the same number of steps, and have the same number of parameters. The training data is built from templates around our sentence (other relatives, other verbs, other sayings). Both models train on the same 5,000 template sentences. Another 500 are kept apart as a test set, and so is our own sentence: the models never see them in training, so they translate them for the first time. Every word in them appears in training, but in other combinations.

Where the weights come from

    Why tía for “aunt”? Nobody wrote this rule. Training adjusted the weights until, after “an”, the new state matched the vector at tía (with 16 or 64 dimensions). Section 7 shows such training.

    The shading on each Galician word is the weight of the encoder's vector after reading that word. That vector also carries the words before it, so a weight on miña can bring in tía as well.

    Exactly right, out of 500 test sentences (not in the training data)

    Where the model with attention looked

    One row per English word it wrote, one column per Galician word; darker means more weight. Each column is the encoder's vector after reading that word, so it also carries the words before it. The model without attention has no such grid, because it uses the same summary vector for every English word.

    Words in red are not in the correct translation; struck-through words are missing. Real sentences hold much more than these templates: with 64 dimensions, one vector holds this toy data perfectly, but real models of 2014 lost details in long sentences (Cho et al. 2014; Bahdanau et al. 2015). Attention solved this without making the vector bigger.

    5A real model on our sentence

    The same arithmetic inside a trained Galician–English model, Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-gl-en. Its decoder has 6 layers with 8 attention heads each, and every head looks back at the source in its own way. Click an output word, or play the translation, to see where the model looked. It writes “An aunt of mine”: correct, but rare in English (translation page, sections 3 to 5).

    Source (Galician), shaded by attention weight

    Output (English), as the model wrote it

    The whole grid: one row per output word, one column per source word

    Words are split into pieces the model knows, such as solucion·aba. ‹/s› marks the end of the sentence; models often park attention there when nothing in the source is needed.

    6Self-attention, and many heads at once

    The encoder uses the same mechanism inside one sentence: every Galician word attends to every Galician word, itself included. Each head has its own queries and keys, so each head learns its own pattern. The heads' outputs are then combined into one vector per word.

    Pick a head, then click a word.

    7Who decides what a head does?

    Nobody. The people who build a model choose how many layers and heads it has, how big they are, and what it is trained to predict. They do not assign jobs to heads. Every head starts as random numbers, and training nudges all of them at once in whatever direction lowers the error. A head ends up with a job because, from its own random start, doing that job was the quickest way down. Researchers find the jobs afterwards, by looking, as we do here.

    Below, a tiny model with 2 layers of 2 heads learns the classic sentence The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired: it has to say what “it” refers to. The adjective decides: tired means the animal, wide means the street. It trains on 96 such sentences. The three runs differ only in their random start.

    Where “it” looks, in each head, for two sentences

    Loss (lower is better) and the current step

    The job each head ended up with, over all 96 sentences

    Layer 1 lets every word look at every word; layer 2 looks from “it” and names the referent. Keys and queries have 2 dimensions. Adam, learning rate 0.03, 500 steps. “Switched off” means that head's output is set to zero after training. “Other words” are the, didn't, cross, because, was: models often use such positions to store or park information.
